h1:
Mekong River Fish in Nakhon Phanom
10 Riverside Spots, Laos Views
intro: Nakhon Phanom keeps its best food under the surface of the Mekong — pla khang, pla pho, soft-fleshed river fish, all caught and cooked fresh right at the water's edge. Eating river fish is just everyday life here, and the good spots cluster along the riverbank where you can catch the cool breeze and look across at the Laos mountains as a backdrop. We've picked places both in town and out of town that are genuinely still open, and we'll tell you straight which one suits which kind of meal.

blocks.html: Mekong River fish is nothing like farmed fish — the flesh is firmer, the muddy smell is fainter, and several species are hard to find outside the area. The one locals in Nakhon Phanom talk about most is pla khang (Asian redtail catfish), chewy and rich, great in tom yum or stir-fried with chilli and basil. Then there's pla pho, soft and silky, the favourite for dropping into a hot-pot. And soft-fleshed river fish, thin-bodied and deep-fried whole with garlic until crisp. Fish here runs by season and the price moves with whatever was caught that day, so ask the restaurant what's fresh before you order.

blocks.text: What kinds of Mekong fish are there to eat

items: Pla khang (Asian redtail catfish) — firm and chewy, nicely rich, the star of tom yum and chilli-basil stir-fries. Mid-range price, on nearly every menu.
Pla pho — soft and silky, similar to iridescent shark catfish; locals love it in hot-pot or fried with fish sauce.
Soft-fleshed river fish — thin-bodied, deep-fried whole with garlic until crisp; you'll snack on it like a starter.
Pla buek (giant Mekong catfish) — big fish with lots of meat; some places do a tom yum with it, but not every day, so ask first.
Pla khae / pla jok — local fish that take well to larb and steamed-with-lime, bold and full of flavour.

blocks.title: Before you order
blocks.html: River fish runs by season and by the tide — some days the pla khang is gone but the pla pho has come in. Ask what's fresh today, then pick your dishes around what they've got. That's how you end up with the best of the day.

blocks.text: 10 riverside fish spots locals actually go to

items.name: Rat Rim Khong
items.blurb: A homely spot right on the bank, out of town toward Tha Uthen, about 5 km out, with seating up top and huts down at the water where the breeze never stops. The strong suits are the fish hot-pot in tangy sour-curry broth and the fried-fish miang wraps — fresh ingredients, a cook who knows what they're doing. Locals call it the fish place they never skip, however many times they go.
items.meta: Out of town, toward Tha Uthen · late morning–evening

items.name: Pen Pla Pen
items.blurb: One of the most talked-about river-fish places, sitting on the Mekong along the Nakhon Phanom–Tha Uthen road. The menu runs long — pla pho hot-pot, tom yum pla khang, pla khae larb, pla pho fried with fish sauce, and pla jok steamed with lime, all bold, full-on Isan flavour. Easygoing in the evening with a cool river breeze.
items.meta: Nakhon Phanom–Tha Uthen Rd, Aat Samat · late morning–evening

items.name: Phu Tawan Pla Jum
items.blurb: A riverside fish hot-pot place in town. The headliner is the pla pho hot-pot — soft fish dipped and eaten with a spicy jaew dip — with oyster yum and shrimp marinated in fish sauce on the side. Good for a bigger group gathered around the pot for a long, slow meal.

items.name: Sabaidee@Nakhon Phanom
items.blurb: A river-fish place in town with plenty of fish to choose from — walk over, look, and point at the one you want. The standouts are pla khang stir-fried with chilli and basil, pla khang larb, and pla khang hot-pot. Serious fish fans say they leave happy.

items.name: Suan Ahan View Khong
items.blurb: A garden restaurant on Sunthon Wichit Road near Fortune River View Hotel, comfortable seating with a full Mekong view. The fish menu covers the lot — tom yum pla buek, fried tilapia, and pla khang stir-fried with chilli and basil. Good for a family meal where you want both the view and roomy seating.
items.meta: Sunthon Wichit Rd, in town · late morning–evening

items.name: Rabiang Khong
items.blurb: A riverside spot near the walking street, with terrace seating where you see the Mekong and the Laos side clearly. The river-fish menu has pla buek, pla khang and pla jok, plus shrimp and squid. Good for an evening meet-up before you carry on to the night market.
items.meta: Near the walking street, riverside · dinner

items.name: Khrua Rim Khong View, That Phanom
items.blurb: If you head down toward That Phanom, this is the place to stop for fish. The standouts are tom yum with Mekong fish, choo chee pla khang, and soft-fleshed fish fried with garlic. You eat with a quiet river view here — a different mood from the spots in town.
items.meta: That Phanom district, riverside · late morning–evening

items.name: Pla Jum Chom Khong
items.blurb: A fish hot-pot place that does what the name says — gather around the pot and dip fresh fish at the river's edge, with a well-balanced broth and a jaew dip. Prices are friendly. Good for a group of friends after a relaxed, no-fuss meal.

items.name: Ban Nam Phong (near the Naga plaza)
items.blurb: Sitting near the Phaya Sri Sattanakharat Naga plaza, walkable from the riverside. Strong on som tam and fried dishes, with river-fish options on the side. Good for a stop before or after taking photos at the Naga.
items.meta: Near the Naga plaza, in town · midday–evening

items.name: The Tree Cafe and Restaurant
items.blurb: A spot on Sunthon Wichit Road that blends a cafe with full meals — good for a group that doesn't go heavy on the spice. There's fried featherback fish cake, squid stir-fried with salted egg, and one-plate dishes. You can sit by the river and linger.
items.meta: Sunthon Wichit Rd, in town · midday–evening

blocks.text: Fish dishes to order for the full range of flavours

blocks.html: If there are a few of you, try to cover the full range like this — start with tom yum pla khang, a clear broth, bold and sour-forward, then move to pla pho hot-pot, dipping piece by piece into a hot jaew dip, and finish with crisp soft-fleshed fish fried with garlic and a bold-flavoured fish larb to eat with sticky rice. Soup, grilled, and fried, all in one meal.

items.name: Tom yum pla khang
items.blurb: Clear, bold broth — sour, spicy and well balanced, with chewy pla khang. The opening dish nearly every place here does well.

items.name: Pla pho hot-pot
items.blurb: Soft, silky pla pho dipped till cooked and eaten with jaew. Best shared, a group gathered around the pot.

items.name: Soft-fleshed fish fried with garlic
items.blurb: Fried crisp whole, fragrant with garlic — a snackable dish that kids will eat too.

items.name: Fish larb / steamed fish with lime
items.blurb: Bold, full-on Isan flavour, sour and spicy — eat the whole plate with sticky rice.

blocks.text: Which places get the Laos mountain view

blocks.html: The charm of Nakhon Phanom's fish places is the backdrop — across the water is the Lao town of Thakhek, with a line of mountains behind it. In the late afternoon, once the sun softens, the breeze off the river is cool and easy. The spots with the full view are the ones right on the bank — Rat Rim Khong, Rabiang Khong, and Suan Ahan View Khong. Plenty of places in town also look across Sunthon Wichit Road to the Mekong.

blocks.title: Best time of day
blocks.html: Go from late afternoon to sunset, around 5:00–6:30 pm, for both the good light and the cool breeze. The popular places get busy on weekends, so if you're a group, call ahead to reserve a table by the water.

blocks.text: Things to know before you go

items: Many riverside places are about the atmosphere, sit-and-eat spots; evenings get busy and food may come out slowly, so allow extra time.
Fish is priced by the fish and by weight; big fish like pla buek can cost more than you'd expect, so ask the price before ordering and you'll feel better about it.
Out-of-town spots like Rat Rim Khong and the That Phanom side are easier to reach by car than by public transport — if you have a car, drive yourself.
Fresh fish sells out fast and some prized species are limited per day, so if there's a particular fish you've got your eye on, don't go too late.

faq.q: Which Mekong fish restaurant in Nakhon Phanom is the best?
faq.a: Locals talk most about Rat Rim Khong and Pen Pla Pen. Rat Rim Khong stands out for its fish hot-pot in tangy sour-curry broth and its homely riverbank atmosphere, while Pen Pla Pen has a wide fish menu — pla pho hot-pot, tom yum pla khang and fish larb — with bold, full-on Isan flavour.

faq.q: Which Mekong fish should I try?
faq.a: Pla khang is firm and chewy, great in tom yum and chilli-basil stir-fries; pla pho is soft and good for hot-pot; and soft-fleshed river fish is fried crisp whole with garlic. These three are the stars you'll find at nearly every riverside spot.

faq.q: About how much do riverside fish restaurants in Nakhon Phanom cost?
faq.a: Most run around THB 150–350 per head if you order a few dishes. Fish hot-pot places like Phu Tawan Pla Jum can climb to THB 250–500 per head. Fish is priced by the fish and by weight, and a big pla buek will cost more, so ask the price before you order.

faq.q: What time gives the best view at the riverside fish spots?
faq.a: Late afternoon to sunset, around 5:00–6:30 pm, gives both the good light and the cool breeze off the river, with the line of Laos mountains as a backdrop. Weekends get busy, so book a table by the water ahead of time.

faq.q: Which fish restaurants have a view of the Laos mountains?
faq.a: The ones right on the bank with the full view are Rat Rim Khong, Rabiang Khong, and Suan Ahan View Khong. Across the water is the Lao town of Thakhek with its mountains as a backdrop. Many places in town along Sunthon Wichit Road can see the Mekong too.
